slides: In the last question, the shaded triangle was exactly as big as the two white triangles together. Let's take that idea and stretch it.

slides.say: A rectangle, and a diagonal in it. The diagonal cuts the rectangle into two triangles, and they are exactly the same size. So the shaded half equals the white half, and each one is half of the rectangle. That's clear to all of us.

Now a shaded triangle inside a rectangle, like in the last question. Its base is the bottom side, and its tip, E, is on the top side. Here too, the shaded part is half of the rectangle, and the white parts together are the other half.
Why? From E, drop a height down to the bottom side. It cuts the rectangle into two smaller rectangles, and each small rectangle has a diagonal.
In the left rectangle, the shaded piece and the white piece are the two halves, so they're equal. In the right rectangle too. So each shaded piece equals its white twin.
And it doesn't matter where E is along the top side. Move it, and the shaded triangle is still half of the rectangle.
It's true here as well. It doesn't matter how many triangles there are inside the rectangle, as long as their bases fill the bottom side, one after the other, and their tips are on the top side.
at: their tips are on the top side

slides.say: Then the shaded parts always add up to the white parts, and each is half of the rectangle.

By the way, this isn't only true in a rectangle. It's true in the whole parallelogram family: a parallelogram, a rectangle, a rhombus and a square. A diagonal in a parallelogram also cuts it into two triangles with the same area.
And this one? A shaded triangle on the bottom side of a parallelogram, with its tip on the top side. It's harder to see, but from the tip, draw a line parallel to the slanted sides.

Now we have two parallelograms, a left one and a right one. In each of them, the shaded piece and the white piece are the two halves. So the shaded triangle is half of the whole parallelogram. Same base and same height, and it doesn't matter how many triangles.
A slightly more advanced one. The bottom side is cut into four equal pieces. The shaded triangle stands on one piece, and its tip is on the top side. What part of the rectangle is it?

A triangle on the whole bottom side, with its tip on the top side, would be half of the rectangle. Ours has the same height, but it stands on only a quarter of the bottom side. So it's a quarter of that half.
at: A triangle on the whole bottom side
So it's a quarter of that half

slides.say: A quarter of a half is an eighth. So the shaded triangle is an eighth of the rectangle.

slides: This symmetry principle is very important. Some exam questions become easy with it, and we'll see one in the next question. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
